slides.0.title: Viticulture and climate
slides.0.subtitle: Frost, hail, the Zonda wind, water rights and drought, organic and sustainable practice
slides.1.title: The main climate hazards
slides.1.highlights.0.title: Hail
slides.1.highlights.0.content: Hail is a major risk in Mendoza, with several studies of its hailstorms and the large damage they cause (e.g. Pérez & Puliafito 2006; Bechis et al. 2022); anti-hail netting is common in many areas such as San Rafael
slides.1.highlights.1.title: Frost
slides.1.highlights.1.content: Frost can hit high valleys (WSET study material); the higher the planting, the more frost has to be watched
slides.1.highlights.2.title: The Zonda and heatwaves
slides.1.highlights.2.content: The summer Zonda is a hazard; heatwaves in the lowlands are driving growers up the Andean slopes (journal abstract)
slides.1.content: Argentina's risks are extremes — hail, frost, heatwaves and heavy rain — rather than persistent wet pressure.
slides.2.title: Water: irrigation, rights and drought
slides.2.highlights.0.title: Irrigation is essential
slides.2.highlights.0.content: Most vineyards lie in the Andean rain shadow with very little rain; irrigation was historically by flood and is moving to drip; water control and stress management are a quality lever
slides.2.highlights.1.title: Water rights and governance
slides.2.highlights.1.content: Water availability and governance in Mendoza is a research topic of its own (Castex et al. 2015); the details of water rights must be checked in official sources
slides.2.highlights.2.title: Drought
slides.2.highlights.2.content: Research describes a decade-long hydrological drought in central-western Argentina (Rivera et al. 2021)
slides.2.content: Snowmelt is the lifeline: the gap between snowy and drought years is the gap in yield and style.
slides.3.title: Climate change and adaptation
slides.3.highlights.0.title: Already happening
slides.3.highlights.0.content: The journal abstract finds from past decades of data that climate change is already occurring; extreme rainfall can also degrade land and endanger vineyards
slides.3.highlights.1.title: Moving upslope
slides.3.highlights.1.content: One adaptation is moving higher and cooler: Chandon's sparkling vineyards in Gualtallary went from 1,250 m in 1990 to 1,625 m in 2015 (The Drinks Business, 2019)
slides.3.highlights.2.title: Organic and sustainable
slides.3.highlights.2.content: The dry climate keeps disease pressure low, which suits organic viticulture; certification and area figures must be checked in official statistics and are not quoted here
slides.3.content: Adapting to climate change means going to higher altitudes and managing water better.
What characterises the hazards of Argentine vineyards?
A. Extreme events: hail, frost, heatwaves, heavy rain
Mostly extreme events; disease pressure is low.
Chandon's sparkling vineyards in Gualtallary rose from 1,250 m in 1990 to what by 2015?
A. From flood irrigation increasingly to drip
What are lowland heatwaves driving growers to do?
A. Move to higher Andean slopes
